question: Inhibin: a new circulating marker of hydatidiform mole?
answer: Serum inhibin was significantly elevated in patients with complete hydatidiform mole before evacuation (median 8.3 U/ml) compared with normal pregnant women at the same stage (2.8 U/ml), and it fell to follicular-phase levels (0.4 U/ml) 7-10 days after evacuation, supporting inhibin as a circulating marker of mole. Molar tissue contained very high inhibin concentrations (cytosol median 578 U/ml), consistent with the tissue being a source of the circulating inhibin. None of the four patients whose post-evacuation serum inhibin was 0.4 U/ml or less developed persistent trophoblastic disease, suggesting a possible prognostic role. In patients with molar/placental tumours, serum inhibin A was elevated in 10/17 patients and inhibin B in 4/17, and inhibin A tracked HCG and HCGbeta during chemotherapy, normalizing faster than HCG in some patients; inhibin B did not correlate with HCGbeta.

question: Discharging patients earlier from Winnipeg hospitals: does it adversely affect quality of care?
answer: In Winnipeg's seven large acute care hospitals, length of stay fell significantly (11.1% to 22.0%) over 1989-90 to 1992-93 for four diagnostic categories without a consistent rise in 30-day readmission rates or physician visits, so shorter stays did not appear to adversely affect quality of care. Across individual Winnipeg hospitals in 1992-93, length of stay was not significantly correlated with readmission rates in any of the four categories, nor with mean physician visits for AMI and bronchitis or asthma. The one exception was readmission for uterine or adnexal procedures, which rose significantly between the first and second year (p=0.04) and then stayed constant over the next three years. For AMI, physician visits rose slightly in the first year and then stayed the same, and they fell slightly for bronchitis or asthma.

question: Acute respiratory distress syndrome in children with malignancy--can we predict outcome?
answer: In a retrospective review of 17 children with malignancy and ARDS who needed mechanical ventilation, ventilator-derived respiratory measures predicted outcome: peak inspiratory pressure, PEEP and ventilation index separated survivors from non-survivors by day 3. question: Does tranexamic acid reduce desmopressin-induced hyperfibrinolysis?
answer: In a randomized study of 100 CABG patients, adding tranexamic acid to desmopressin reduced fibrinolysis-related markers compared with desmopressin alone: fibrin split products were lower (13.5 vs 21.2 ng/mL) and fibrinogen was higher (167 vs 113 mg/dL), both P=.0001. question: Is specialty care associated with improved survival of patients with congestive heart failure?
answer: In a retrospective VHA cohort of 11,661 CHF patients, those with mixed general medicine and cardiology follow-up had the lowest 1-year mortality (19% unadjusted), and adjusted risk of death was higher with general medicine only (RR 1.26, 1.15-1.38) and with neither clinic (RR 1.48, 1.28-1.72). Cardiology-only follow-up was not significantly different from mixed care in adjusted mortality (RR 1.12, 0.94-1.34), so the survival advantage was seen mainly for care that included cardiology versus general medicine alone. The finding of higher mortality with general medicine only versus mixed care was replicated in a second VHA cohort (RR 1.25, 1.14-1.37).

question: Is breast cancer prognosis inherited?
answer: A Swedish population-based cohort study found that breast cancer prognosis aggregates in families: daughters and sisters of a proband with poor prognosis had a 60% higher 5-year breast cancer mortality than those of a proband with good prognosis (HR 1.6, 95% CI 1.2 to 2.2). question: Is laparoscopic adrenalectomy safe and effective for adrenal masses larger than 7 cm?
answer: In a retrospective series of 18 laparoscopic adrenalectomies for lesions larger than 7 cm (mean 8.3 cm), the procedure was feasible, with a mean operative time of 137 min and mean blood loss of 182 mL. question: Does minimal access major surgery in the newborn hurt less?
answer: In a retrospective matched cohort of neonates undergoing thoracoscopic minimal access surgery for esophageal atresia or congenital diaphragmatic hernia, cumulative opioid doses did not differ significantly from conventional surgery controls at 12, 24, 48 hours or 7 days. question: Does a colonoscopy after acute diverticulitis affect its management?
answer: Evidence on whether colonoscopy after acute diverticulitis changes management is mixed. One study of 100 patients with early colonoscopy found no malignancy and no new or different diagnosis, while another found colon cancer in 2.2% of those who had endoscopic evaluation after CT-diagnosed diverticulitis. In the 100 patients who had colonoscopy 4 to 6 weeks after discharge, 32% had at least one polyp and only one was an advanced adenoma. No colonic malignancy was found, and no new or different diagnosis resulted. In 402 patients with colonic evaluation after CT-diagnosed diverticulitis, 9 (2.2%) had colon cancer and 78 had polyps. Cancer was diagnosed within 6 months of the CT in 8 of the 9 patients. Cancer risk was concentrated in particular CT findings. Odds ratios were 23.35 for mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymph nodes, 4.67 for abscess, and 24.43 for obstruction with a localized mass. Cancer was also associated with the location of the diverticulitis, and the odds were 2.5 times higher in women.

question: Are serum leptin levels a prognostic factor in advanced lung cancer?
answer: In one study of 71 previously untreated lung cancer patients, serum leptin levels showed no association with overall survival, so leptin was not found to be a prognostic factor. In the same study, leptin did not differ significantly by ECOG performance status, weight loss, histological type, disease stage or TNM classification, although it correlated with BMI. Serum leptin was lower in lung cancer patients than in matched controls at diagnosis (4.75 vs 9.67 ng/ml), which is a diagnostic comparison rather than evidence of prognostic value.
